findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Have `_restrict_dir_to_owner` decode whoami output so it cannot fail, e.g. capture bytes and decode with errors="replace" (only the ASCII SID column is used), check that the parsed SID matches `S-1-...`, map any decode or parse failure to OpcertKeyError, and add a portable test with non-ASCII whoami bytes.

keyprov.py:143-149 already uses `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` with the locale codec; copying that pattern for whoami brings strict ANSI decoding of OEM-code-page output with it
findings.finding: The plan says unparseable `whoami` output raises OpcertKeyError, but decoding can fail before parsing. Redirected whoami writes in the console OEM code page, while `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` decodes with the ANSI locale encoding in strict mode. For a domain or user name with non-ASCII characters, this raises UnicodeDecodeError instead of returning text. The existing `except BaseException` still cleans up, but compose fails with a non-OpcertKeyError exception, and signing does not work at all for those users. The SID field the helper needs is always ASCII.
findings.location: Approach — `_restrict_dir_to_owner` bullet (whoami /user /fo csv /nh parsed with csv); Testing — portable failure cases
scenarios: Windows account named e.g. `DOMAIN\Jürgen` or with a CJK username: whoami's OEM-encoded bytes are invalid in cp1252/ANSI, so subprocess raises UnicodeDecodeError and op-cert signing cannot compose for that user
findings.suggested_fix: Run whoami without text=True (or with encoding='ascii', errors='replace'), parse the CSV and take the last field, validate it against r'^S-1-\d+(-\d+)+$', and raise OpcertKeyError('cannot read the current user SID from whoami: ...') when that check fails. Add a portable test that fakes whoami returning non-ASCII bytes in the name column and asserts the SID is still extracted.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Rewrite the icacls rationale to say the repo's only icacls use is the read-only ACL probe in test.yml, and add one sentence on why subprocess icacls/whoami beats an in-process DACL via ctypes (the approach CPython uses for mkdir(0o700)).
evidence: Plan: "`icacls` is the mechanism the repo already uses for Windows ACLs (the sweep's ACL probe step in `.github/workflows/test.yml`)"

Repo: .github/workflows/test.yml:292 `[subprocess.run(['icacls', p], check=False) for p in (d, key, copy_dir)]` — a read-only print of ACLs in the diag step; search_files finds no other icacls use under .github, and keyprov.py has none

Retrieved: CPython issue gh-118486 ('Enable mkdir(mode=0o700) to work on Windows… Switch mkdir(mode=0o700) on Windows to use OWNER RIGHTS') — CPython builds this DACL in-process, not by calling icacls
findings.finding: The plan picks icacls partly because it is 'the mechanism the repo already uses for Windows ACLs', but the repo only uses icacls to print ACLs in a diagnostic workflow step. It has never used icacls to change an ACL, and never from library code. Since the precedent doesn't exist, the plan also never compares its choice with the in-process approach CPython itself takes for mkdir(0o700) (building an SDDL/DACL through the Win32 security API, which Python could reach via ctypes). That approach would avoid parsing whoami's text output and the three subprocess round-trips.
findings.location: Approach — bullet 2 ('icacls is the mechanism the repo already uses for Windows ACLs')
scenarios: A reviewer accepts the subprocess design because they believe it matches existing library code, when the only existing use is a CI diagnostic print
